payload.title: Titration of a weak acid with a strong base

stimulus.description: A student titrates $25\text{ mL}$ of a $0.1\text{ M}$ solution of the weak monoprotic acid $\mathrm{C_{6}H_{5}COOH}$ ($K_a=6.30\times10^{-5}$ at $25^\circ\text{C}$) with $0.2\text{ M}$ NaOH. Indicators available: methyl orange (pH 3.1–4.4); bromocresol green (pH 3.8–5.4); methyl red (pH 4.4–6.2); bromothymol blue (pH 6.0–7.6); phenolphthalein (pH 8.2–10.0); alizarin yellow R (pH 10.1–12.0).

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Write the equilibrium expression and calculate the pH of the acid solution before any NaOH is added.
parts.model_answer: $K_a=[\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{A^-}]/[\mathrm{HA}]$; with $x=[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$, $x^2/(0.1-x)=K_a$ gives $x=0.00248\text{ M}$ and $\mathrm{pH}=2.61$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes $K_a=[\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{A^-}]/[\mathrm{HA}]$ or the equivalent ICE-table expression
Calculates $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$ (about 0.0025 M)
Reports the pH (about 2.61)

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH, in mL, required to reach the equivalence point.
parts.model_answer: moles of acid $0.0025$; $V=12.5\text{ mL}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the moles of acid (0.0025 mol)
common_errors: uses mL without converting to L

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the equivalence volume (about 12.5 mL) with units
common_errors: uses the acid volume as the base volume

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the pH of the solution at the half-equivalence point, and explain how the result is related to the acid.
parts.model_answer: At half-equivalence $[\mathrm{HA}]=[\mathrm{A^-}]$, so $\mathrm{pH}=\mathrm{p}K_a=4.20$.

rubric_rows.criterion: States pH equals $\mathrm{p}K_a$ (4.20) at half-equivalence
Explains that $[\mathrm{HA}]=[\mathrm{A^-}]$ there, so $\log([\mathrm{A^-}]/[\mathrm{HA}])=0$ in the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
common_errors: says the acid is neutralized completely

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Select the most appropriate indicator for this titration from the list and justify your choice.
parts.model_answer: phenolphthalein: the pH at equivalence is about 8.5, inside its color-change range, because the conjugate base of a weak acid makes the equivalence-point solution basic.

rubric_rows.criterion: Selects phenolphthalein
common_errors: selects the indicator closest to pH 7

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with the equivalence-point pH (about 8.5) lying within the indicator range because the solution contains the weak conjugate base

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: The student repeats the titration with the same volume of acid at double the concentration. Does the volume of NaOH needed to reach equivalence change? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Yes, it doubles, because the moles of acid double and the moles of base needed are in a 1:1 ratio.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the equivalence volume doubles because the moles of acid double (1:1 ratio)
common_errors: says it does not change because Ka is unchanged

payload.title: Free energy, equilibrium and a galvanic cell

stimulus.description: For a reaction at $500\text{ K}$: $\Delta H^\circ=-92\text{ kJ/mol}_{rxn}$ and $\Delta S^\circ=-188\text{ J/(mol}_{rxn}\cdot\text{K)}$ (both independent of temperature). Part (d) concerns a different system: a galvanic cell with $\mathrm{Ni}$/$\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Ag}$/$\mathrm{Ag^{+}}$ half-cells, with standard reduction potentials $-0.25\text{ V}$ and $+0.80\text{ V}$ respectively.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Calculate $\Delta G^\circ$, in kJ/mol, for the reaction at $500\text{ K}$.
parts.model_answer: $\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ=2.0\text{ kJ/mol}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses $\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ$ with entropy converted to kJ
Calculates $\Delta G^\circ$ (about 2.0 kJ/mol) with units

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Determine the temperature at which the reaction changes between thermodynamically favorable and unfavorable, and state whether the reaction is favorable above or below that temperature. Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: $\Delta G^\circ=0$ at $T=\Delta H^\circ/\Delta S^\circ=489\text{ K}$; the reaction is favorable below this temperature because $\Delta S^\circ$ is negative.

rubric_rows.criterion: Sets $\Delta G^\circ=0$ and solves $T=\Delta H^\circ/\Delta S^\circ$
Calculates the temperature (about 489 K)
States the reaction is favorable below that temperature, citing the sign of $\Delta S^\circ$ in $\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ$
common_errors: links favorability to the sign of ΔH alone

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the equilibrium constant, $K$, at $500\text{ K}$.
parts.model_answer: $K=e^{-\Delta G^\circ/RT}\approx 0.62$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses $\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K$ with R in J/(mol·K) and ΔG° in joules
common_errors: uses kJ with R in J

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $K$ (about 0.62)

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: On a diagram of the galvanic cell, label the anode and the direction of electron flow, and calculate the standard cell potential.
parts.model_answer: The anode is the half-cell with the less positive reduction potential (Ni2+/Ni); $E^\circ_{cell}=1.05\text{ V}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Labels the Ni2+/Ni half-cell as the anode (more negative reduction potential, where oxidation occurs) and electrons flowing from the anode through the wire to the cathode
common_errors: identifies the more positive half-cell as the anode

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $E^\circ_{cell}=1.05\text{ V}$ (cathode minus anode)

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Calculate $\Delta G^\circ$ for the cell reaction, if 2 moles of electrons are transferred per mole of reaction, and state what the sign of the result indicates.
parts.model_answer: $\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ=-203\text{ kJ/mol}$; the negative value shows the cell reaction is thermodynamically favorable.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $\Delta G^\circ$ (about -203 kJ/mol) and states that the negative sign means favorable

payload.title: Concentration–time data and the order of a reaction

stimulus.description: Concentration of A in the reaction A → products at 310 K

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Determine the order of the reaction with respect to A. Describe the plot you would make and what it would show to support your conclusion.
parts.model_answer: The reaction is first order: a plot of ln[A] versus t is a straight line (the other linearized plots curve).

rubric_rows.criterion: Describes making the plot of ln[A] versus t (and checks at least one other linearization)
Concludes the reaction is first order
common_errors: picks the order whose plot is curved

rubric_rows.criterion: Supports the claim with the linearity of that plot and the curvature of the others

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the rate constant, $k$, with units.
parts.model_answer: $k=|\text{slope}|\approx 0.009\text{ s}^{-1}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $k$ (about 0.009) from the slope magnitude of the linear plot
common_errors: uses a slope from the curved plot

rubric_rows.criterion: Gives the correct units for k ($ s^-1$ form)
common_errors: gives units of a first-order constant for a second-order reaction

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the half-life of the reaction for the initial concentration shown.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses the half-life relation for the identified order
Calculates the half-life (about 77 s)

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The experiment is repeated at a higher temperature. Predict whether $k$ increases, decreases, or is unchanged, and justify your answer using the collision model.
parts.model_answer: $k$ increases: at the higher temperature a larger fraction of collisions has energy at least equal to the activation energy.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that $k$ increases
common_errors: states k decreases because particles collide more often

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with a larger fraction of collisions exceeding the activation energy (and more frequent collisions)

parts.label: E

parts.model_answer: For an elementary step the rate law follows from the reactants of the step. A unimolecular step, A → products, gives rate = k[A], a first-order law, so the step would need to be unimolecular.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the step would have to be unimolecular (one molecule of A) and links the molecularity of an elementary step to the order of 1

payload.title: Photoelectron spectrum of an element

stimulus.description: Photoelectron spectrum of a neutral atom of element X. The height of each peak is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell. Peaks (binding energy in MJ/mol, relative number of electrons): (19.3, 2); (1.36, 2); (0.8, 1).

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify element X and write its complete ground-state electron configuration.
parts.model_answer: The total relative number of electrons is 5, so X is B: 1s$^{2}$ 2s$^{2}$ 2p$^{1}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies X as B with the configuration 1s$^{2}$ 2s$^{2}$ 2p$^{1}$ (electron total 5)

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Explain why the peak at the highest binding energy corresponds to the electrons in the 1s subshell, using Coulomb's law.
parts.model_answer: The 1s electrons are closest to the nucleus, so the attraction is greatest (Coulomb's law: larger force at a smaller distance), so they need the most energy to remove.

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites the smaller distance from the nucleus and the larger Coulombic attraction
common_errors: says 1s electrons are shielded the most

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: On the axes of the spectrum, sketch the peak(s) for the valence electrons of C, which has one more proton than X. State whether they appear at a higher or lower binding energy than the valence peak of X, and justify.
parts.model_answer: The valence peak of C is at a slightly higher binding energy than that of X because the greater nuclear charge acts on electrons in the same shell with little added shielding.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws the valence peak(s) of C at a higher binding energy than X's valence peak, with a justification based on the larger nuclear charge
common_errors: draws the peak at a lower energy

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Is the first ionization energy of C expected to be larger or smaller than that of X? Explain using the spectrum.
parts.model_answer: Generally larger (a larger effective nuclear charge in the same shell), unless the next element's electron is placed in a new subshell or paired, in which case it is smaller; use the configuration to decide.

rubric_rows.criterion: Compares the valence-peak energies of X and the next element and states the relation to the first ionization energy, noting the exception when the electron enters a new subshell or is paired
common_errors: states the ionization energy is the energy of the 1s peak

payload.title: Combustion stoichiometry and gas volume

stimulus.description: A $10\text{ g}$ sample of $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$ is burned completely in excess oxygen, producing $\mathrm{CO_2}(g)$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}(g)$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$, using the smallest whole-number coefficients.
parts.model_answer: The balanced equation is 2C2H6 + 7O2 → 4CO2 + 6H2O.

rubric_rows.criterion: Balanced equation with the smallest whole-number coefficients: 2C2H6 + 7O2 → 4CO2 + 6H2O

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ produced.
parts.model_answer: $n(\mathrm{CO_2})=2\times10/30.07=0.665\text{ mol}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates 0.665 mol using the molar mass of the fuel and the 2:1 mole ratio

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the volume, in L, occupied by the $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ at $127\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $1\text{ atm}$.
parts.model_answer: $V=nRT/P=21.8\text{ L}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the volume (about 21.8 L) using kelvins and consistent R

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: A student claims that this combustion is an oxidation–reduction reaction. Justify the claim using oxidation numbers of one element.
parts.model_answer: Oxygen goes from 0 in $\mathrm{O_2}$ to −2 in the products (reduced), and carbon's oxidation number increases (oxidized).

rubric_rows.criterion: Gives oxidation numbers before and after for oxygen (0 to −2) or carbon (increase) showing electron transfer

payload.title: Lewis structure, geometry and boiling points

stimulus.description: Consider the molecule $\mathrm{CH_{4}}$ and the two compounds $\mathrm{CH_{3}OH}$ and $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: In the box provided, draw a Lewis electron-dot diagram of $\mathrm{CH_{4}}$ that shows all valence electrons.
parts.model_answer: A valid diagram with 4 valence electrons on the central atom group and 4 bonded atoms and 0 lone pair(s) on the central atom.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws a Lewis structure with the correct total valence electrons, 4 bonds to the central atom and 0 lone pair(s) on it
common_errors: omits the lone pairs on the central atom

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Based on your diagram, identify the molecular geometry of $\mathrm{CH_{4}}$ and the approximate bond angle.
parts.model_answer: tetrahedral; bond angle 109.5°.

rubric_rows.criterion: States tetrahedral geometry and a bond angle of 109.5°

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Is the $\mathrm{CH_{4}}$ molecule polar or nonpolar? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Nonpolar: the bond dipoles cancel by symmetry.

rubric_rows.criterion: States nonpolar and links it to symmetric cancellation of the bond dipoles

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The boiling point of $\mathrm{CH_{3}OH}$ is higher than that of $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$. Explain the difference in terms of intermolecular forces.
parts.model_answer: The compound with the higher boiling point has the stronger intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonding or stronger dispersion/dipole attractions), which need more energy to overcome.

rubric_rows.criterion: Names the stronger intermolecular force of CH3OH (hydrogen bonding where an N–H, O–H, or F–H bond is present, otherwise stronger dispersion) as the reason
common_errors: says covalent bonds break on boiling

review.summary: The bundle is a set of four loosely connected 1-point recall parts on CH4, not a 4-point short FRQ built around topic 2.7. The scoring, wording and misconception coverage also have problems, so it fails on four of the five criteria.

scope_skill.notes: Part A is a plain Lewis diagram of CH4 (skill 3.B, topic 2.5). Part B is a routine VSEPR recall of tetrahedral and 109.5° for CH4, which is trivial. Part C (polarity) and Part D (intermolecular forces, topic 3.1) are recall rather than model analysis. Hybridization is never assessed. The dominant demand is not 4.A on 2.7, and nothing links the parts to a single model-analysis question.

key_scoring.notes: Part A's model answer is generic template text ("4 valence electrons on the central atom group... 0 lone pair(s)"), and its common error ("omits the lone pairs on the central atom") makes no sense for CH4, which has none. The rubric requires "all valence electrons", but a diagram with four bonds could be scored either way. The D1 criterion lists hydrogen bonding in a template-conditional way. It also lets a stronger-dispersion answer in as an alternative, which would be wrong for CH3OH. The D1 required element is only "hydrogen bonding". Parts C and D are written as 1-point justifications, but their rubrics are thin. The stimulus data is empty.

stimulus_expression.notes: The stem says "Consider the molecule CH4 and the two compounds CH3OH and C2H6" with an empty data object. Part A says "in the box provided" without a box being specified. The stimulus is a plain list of formulas and does not support any real analysis. Part D should give the molar masses or make clear that dispersion forces are comparable.

distractor_explanation.notes: This is a free-response item, so there are no distractors. The listed common errors are generic and partly irrelevant, for example the lone-pair error for CH4 and "reports the electron-domain geometry", which is identical to the molecular geometry for CH4. The misconceptions list is empty.

difficultyRationale: Four short parts spanning K expression, Q vs K direction, a volume disturbance (gas mole comparison or Q reasoning) and temperature effect on K via the sign of delta H. Each part needs 1-2 steps with simple arithmetic (Q = 0.02), but together they require choosing the governing relationship and justifying claims with chemical principles. This is typical of an AP free-response equilibrium question and appropriate for a full mock. It is not advanced because there is no ICE table, there are no coupled equilibria and the arithmetic is minimal.

payload.title: Equilibrium expression, Q versus K and disturbances

stimulus.description: At a certain temperature the equilibrium $\mathrm{A}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\,\mathrm{B}(g)$ has $K_c=0.2$ and is endothermic. A rigid flask initially contains $[\mathrm{A}]=0.5\text{ M}$ and $[\mathrm{B}]=0.1\text{ M}$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Write the equilibrium-constant expression, $K_c$, for the reaction.
parts.model_answer: $K_c=[\mathrm{B}]^2/[\mathrm{A}]$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes $[\mathrm{B}]^2/[\mathrm{A}]$ (products over reactant, with the coefficient as an exponent)

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the reaction quotient, $Q$, for the initial mixture and determine the direction in which the reaction proceeds.
parts.model_answer: $Q=0.02$, which is less than $K_c$, so the reaction proceeds toward the products.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $Q\approx 0.02$ and states the direction as forward by comparing Q with K
common_errors: reverses the comparison of Q and K

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The volume of the flask is doubled at constant temperature after the system reaches equilibrium. Predict the direction of the shift and justify.
parts.model_answer: The system shifts toward the products because the side with more moles of gas is favored at lower pressure ($Q<K$ right after the expansion).

rubric_rows.criterion: States the shift toward the products with the argument that expansion lowers the pressure and favors more moles of gas (Q becomes less than K)

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The temperature is increased. Does the value of $K_c$ increase or decrease? Justify using the sign of the enthalpy change.
parts.model_answer: $K_c$ increases: for an endothermic reaction, heat acts as a reactant, so raising the temperature favors the products.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that $K_c$ increases because heat behaves as a reactant in an endothermic reaction
common_errors: says K does not depend on temperature
